Anatomy-02.question: ১) Circle of Willis is formed by following except-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The Circle of Willis is an arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain that provides collateral cerebral circulation.

It is formed by:

  • Anterior cerebral arteries (right & left)

  • Anterior communicating artery

  • Internal carotid arteries (terminal parts)

  • Posterior communicating arteries (right & left)

  • Posterior cerebral arteries (right & left) (terminal branches of the basilar artery)

Why the options are correct/incorrect:

  • ক) Basilar artery – Although the basilar artery itself is not a component of the ring, it terminates by dividing into the posterior cerebral arteries, which form part of the Circle of Willis. In many anatomy MCQs, the basilar artery is accepted as being associated with the formation of the circle.

  • খ) Anterior and posterior communicating artery – Correct components of the Circle of Willis.

  • গ) Pontine artery – Correct answer (Exception). Pontine arteries are branches of the basilar artery supplying the pons and do not contribute to the Circle of Willis.

  • ঘ) Posterior cerebral artery – Component of the Circle of Willis.

High-Yield Recall

Components of the Circle of Willis (7 arterial segments):

  • 2 Anterior cerebral arteries (A1 segments)

  • 1 Anterior communicating artery

  • 2 Internal carotid arteries

  • 2 Posterior communicating arteries

  • 2 Posterior cerebral arteries (P1 segments)

Anatomy-02.question: ২) Most superficial layer of cerebrum
Anatomy-02.exp:
The cerebral cortex consists of 6 layers (from superficial to deep):

  1. Molecular layer (Layer I) ← Most superficial

  2. External granular layer (Layer II)

  3. External pyramidal layer (Layer III)

  4. Internal granular layer (Layer IV)

  5. Internal pyramidal (ganglionic) layer (Layer V)

  6. Multiform (polymorphic/fusiform) layer (Layer VI)

Why the options are correct/incorrect:

  • ক) Molecular – ✅ Correct. It is the outermost (Layer I) of the cerebral cortex.

  • খ) External granular – Layer II, not the most superficial.

  • গ) External pyramidal – Layer III.

  • ঘ) Multiform – Layer VI, the deepest layer.

High-Yield Recall

Mnemonic (Superficial → Deep):
Men Eat Eggs In International Markets

  • M – Molecular (I)

  • E – External granular (II)

  • E – External pyramidal (III)

  • I – Internal granular (IV)

  • I – Internal pyramidal (V)

  • M – Multiform

Anatomy-02.question: ৩) Layer of epidermis only present in thick skin
৪) Dermatome of umbilicus
৫) Cross section of midbrain at inferior colliculus level shows following except-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is oculomotor nerve. A cross-section of the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus (lower midbrain) shows structures related to the trochlear nerve (CN IV), not the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

The other options are present at this level:

  • Substantia nigra – Present in the midbrain, separating the crus cerebri (ventral) from the tegmentum (dorsal).

  • Rubrospinal tract – Present in the midbrain tegmentum, arising from the red nucleus.

  • Mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve – Extends through the midbrain and is present at this level.

Why oculomotor nerve is incorrect:

  • The oculomotor nucleus and nerve are located at the level of the superior colliculus (upper midbrain).

  • The inferior colliculus level is associated with the trochlear nerve (CN IV), which exits dorsally.

High-yield points:

Midbrain levels:

Superior colliculus level:

  • Oculomotor nucleus (CN III)

  • Red nucleus

  • Substantia nigra

Inferior colliculus level:

  • Trochlear nucleus (CN IV)

  • Decussation of superior cerebellar peduncle

  • Substantia nigra

  • Red nucleus region

Anatomy-02.question: ৬) Tumor involving cervical sympathetic trunk results-
Anatomy-02.option4: Loss of sweating on contralateral side
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is Mydriasis. A tumor involving the cervical sympathetic trunk causes interruption of sympathetic innervation to the eye, producing Horner syndrome. However, the given options contain a terminology issue: damage to the sympathetic pathway causes miosis (pupil constriction), not mydriasis.

Let's evaluate the options:

  • Meiosis (miosis) – This is actually the classic finding in cervical sympathetic trunk lesion due to loss of sympathetic supply to the dilator pupillae muscle.
    (The option likely intended “miosis” rather than “meiosis”)

  • Mydriasis – Incorrect. Mydriasis occurs due to sympathetic stimulation or parasympathetic denervation, not sympathetic trunk damage.

  • Exophthalmos – Not a feature of Horner syndrome. Loss of sympathetic tone may cause apparent enophthalmos.

  • Loss of sweating on contralateral side – Incorrect. The loss of sweating (anhidrosis) occurs on the ipsilateral side of the lesion.

High-yield points:

Cervical sympathetic trunk lesion → Horner syndrome:

  • Miosis

  • Ptosis

  • Anhidrosis (ipsilateral)

  • Apparent enophthalmos

Sympathetic pathway:
Hypothalamus → Brainstem → Cervical spinal cord → Sympathetic chain → Eye

Anatomy-02.question: ৭) Two cerebral hemispheres are connected to each other by the
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is corpus callosum. The corpus callosum is the largest commissural fibre bundle that connects the right and left cerebral hemispheres, allowing communication and transfer of information between corresponding cortical areas.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Internal capsule – Contains projection fibres connecting the cerebral cortex with lower structures such as the thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord. It does not connect the two cerebral hemispheres.

  • Uncinate fasciculus – Connects the frontal lobe and anterior temporal lobe within the same hemisphere.

  • Cingulum – A long association fibre tract within each hemisphere connecting parts of the limbic system (e.g., cingulate gyrus and parahippocampal region).

High-yield points:

Types of cerebral white matter fibres:

  • Commissural fibres → Connect the two hemispheres

    • Corpus callosum (largest)

    • Anterior commissure

  • Association fibres → Connect areas within the same hemisphere

    • Uncinate fasciculus

    • Cingulum

  • Projection fibres → Connect cortex with subcortical structures

    • Internal capsule

Anatomy-02.question: ৮) Which one is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is hippocampus. The hippocampus is a major structure of the medial temporal lobe involved in the consolidation of recent memory into long-term memory. Damage to the hippocampus causes difficulty in forming new memories (anterograde amnesia).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Amygdala – Involved in emotional processing, especially fear and emotional memory, but not the main structure for converting short-term memory into long-term memory.

  • Putamen – A component of the basal ganglia involved in motor control and procedural learning.

  • Pallidum (globus pallidus) – Part of the basal ganglia involved mainly in regulation of movement.

High-yield points:

  • Hippocampus → Consolidation of short-term memory into long-term memory

  • Hippocampal lesion → Anterograde amnesia

  • Amygdala → Fear and emotional memory

  • Basal ganglia (putamen + pallidum) → Motor control and procedural memory

Anatomy-02.question: ৯) Most numerous papillae of tongue
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is filiform papillae. Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the tongue and are distributed over the anterior two-thirds of the dorsal surface. They are conical, keratinized projections that provide a rough surface and help in manipulation of food.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fungiform papillae – Mushroom-shaped papillae scattered mainly on the tip and margins of the tongue. They contain taste buds but are fewer in number.

  • Circumvallate papillae – Largest papillae but few in number (usually 8–12), arranged in a V-shaped row anterior to the sulcus terminalis. They contain many taste buds.

  • Foliate papillae – Located on the posterolateral margins of the tongue; contain taste buds but are less prominent in humans.

High-yield points:

  • Most numerous papillae → Filiform

  • Largest papillae → Circumvallate

  • Most taste buds → Circumvallate

  • Papillae without taste buds → Filiform

  • Taste buds present in → Fungiform, circumvallate, foliate

Anatomy-02.question: ১০) Limbic system excludes-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is basal ganglia. The basal ganglia are not a part of the limbic system; they are primarily involved in motor control, movement regulation, and procedural learning.

The other options are components associated with the limbic system:

  • Anterior thalamic nucleus – Part of the Papez circuit and involved in memory and emotional processing.

  • Mammillary body – A component of the limbic system and part of the Papez circuit, important in memory processing.

  • Hippocampal formation – A major limbic structure involved in memory consolidation, especially conversion of recent memory into long-term memory.

High-yield points:

Major components of limbic system:

  • Hippocampus

  • Amygdala

  • Cingulate gyrus

  • Parahippocampal gyrus

  • Mammillary bodies

  • Anterior thalamic nuclei

  • Septal nuclei

  • Fornix

Basal ganglia:

  • Caudate nucleus

  • Putamen

  • Globus pallidus
    → Mainly involved in motor regulation

Anatomy-02.question: ১১) Effects of lesion of crossed fibres of optic chiasma-
Anatomy-02.option2: Loss of temporal field of vision
Anatomy-02.option3: Loss of nasal field of vision
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is bitemporal hemianopia. The crossed fibres of the optic chiasma are the nasal retinal fibres from both eyes. These fibres carry information from the temporal visual fields. A lesion affecting these crossing fibres results in loss of both temporal visual fields, producing bitemporal hemianopia.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Right homonymous hemianopia – Occurs due to a lesion of the left optic tract, optic radiation, or visual cortex, affecting the same side of the visual field in both eyes.

  • Loss of temporal field of vision – This describes the visual deficit but the specific clinical term is bitemporal hemianopia.

  • Loss of nasal field of vision – Occurs with lesions of the uncrossed temporal retinal fibres, not the optic chiasma crossing fibres.

High-yield points:

Optic pathway lesions:

  • Optic nerve lesion → Ipsilateral blindness

  • Optic chiasma lesion → Bitemporal hemianopia

  • Optic tract lesion → Contralateral homonymous hemianopia

  • Optic radiation lesion → Contralateral homonymous hemianopia

  • Visual cortex lesion → Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (often with macular sparing)

Key concept:

  • Nasal retinal fibres cross at optic chiasma → carry temporal visual fields

  • Damage to crossed fibres → loss of temporal fields of both eyes → bitemporal hemianopia

Anatomy-02.question: ১২) Tracts passing through the genu of the internal capsule-
Anatomy-02.option3: Anterior part of superior thalamic radiation
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is anterior part of superior thalamic radiation. The genu of the internal capsule contains mainly corticobulbar fibres and fibres of the anterior part of superior thalamic radiation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Corticospinal tract – Passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, not the genu. It carries motor fibres from the cortex to the spinal cord.

  • Superior thalamic radiation – The fibres are distributed mainly through the anterior and posterior limbs of the internal capsule. The anterior part is related to the genu region.

  • Auditory radiation – Passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule, below the lentiform nucleus.

High-yield points:

Internal capsule parts and contents:

  • Anterior limb

    • Frontopontine fibres

    • Anterior thalamic radiation

  • Genu

    • Corticobulbar fibres

    • Anterior part of superior thalamic radiation

  • Posterior limb

    • Corticospinal fibres

    • Somatosensory thalamocortical fibres

  • Sublentiform part

    • Auditory radiation

  • Retrolentiform part

    • Optic radiation

Anatomy-02.question: ১৩) Basal ganglia includes-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The question asks which structure is not included in the basal ganglia. The correct answer is red nucleus.

The basal ganglia are a group of deep grey matter nuclei involved mainly in motor control and regulation of movement.

Components include:

  • Corpus striatum – True. It consists of:

    • Caudate nucleus

    • Putamen

  • Subthalamic nucleus – True. It is a functional component of the basal ganglia and is involved in the indirect pathway of movement control.

  • Substantia nigra – True. It is considered a functional part of the basal ganglia; dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta modulate striatal activity.

  • Red nucleus – Incorrect. It is a part of the midbrain tegmentum and is involved in motor coordination via the rubrospinal tract, but it is not a basal ganglia structure.

High-yield points:

Basal ganglia components:

  • Caudate nucleus

  • Putamen

  • Globus pallidus

  • Subthalamic nucleus

  • Substantia nigra

Not part of basal ganglia:

  • Red nucleus

  • Thalamus

  • Cerebellum

Anatomy-02.question: ১৪) Parts of midbrain-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is crus cerebri. The midbrain (mesencephalon) is the uppermost part of the brainstem and consists of:

  • Tectum (dorsal part) containing superior and inferior colliculi

  • Tegmentum (central part)

  • Crus cerebri / cerebral peduncles (ventral part)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pons – It is another part of the brainstem, located between the midbrain and medulla oblongata, but is not a part of the midbrain.

  • Cerebellum – A separate hindbrain structure involved in coordination and balance.

  • Medulla oblongata – The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.

High-yield points:

Brainstem parts (superior to inferior):

  • Midbrain

  • Pons

  • Medulla oblongata

Midbrain structures:

  • Crus cerebri

  • Tegmentum

  • Tectum (superior and inferior colliculi)

Anatomy-02.question: ১৫) Cells of the cerebral cortex exclude-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is Purkinje cells. Purkinje cells are the characteristic neurons of the cerebellar cortex, not the cerebral cortex.

The main neuronal types found in the cerebral cortex include:

  • Pyramidal cells – Major projection neurons of the cerebral cortex; their axons form important descending pathways such as corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.

  • Stellate cells – Small interneurons mainly found in the granular layers of the cerebral cortex.

  • Fusiform cells – Located mainly in the deeper cortical layers and contribute to cortical output pathways.

The incorrect option:

  • Purkinje cells – Found in the cerebellar cortex, arranged in a single layer between the molecular and granular layers; they provide the main output of the cerebellar cortex.

High-yield points:

Cerebral cortex neurons:

  • Pyramidal cells

  • Stellate cells

  • Fusiform cells

Cerebellar cortex characteristic cell:

  • Purkinje cell

Purkinje cell function:

  • Inhibitory output neuron

  • Uses GABA

  • Projects to deep cerebellar nuclei

Anatomy-02.question: ১৬) Features of veins excludes
১৭) Smooth part of right ventricle is developed from
১৮) Right border is mainly formed by
১৯) Cells contributing to the formation of blood brain barrier are-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is astrocytes. Astrocytes contribute to the formation and maintenance of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) by extending their perivascular end-feet around cerebral capillaries and supporting the tight junctions between endothelial cells.

The main components of the blood–brain barrier are:

  • Capillary endothelial cells with tight junctions

  • Basement membrane

  • Astrocyte end-feet

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pale cells – Not a recognized component of the blood–brain barrier.

  • Ependymal cells – Line the ventricles and central canal; involved in cerebrospinal fluid circulation and choroid plexus formation, not BBB formation.

  • Oligodendrocytes – Form myelin in the central nervous system; they do not contribute to the BBB.

High-yield points:

Blood–brain barrier components:

  • Non-fenestrated endothelial cells

  • Tight junctions

  • Basement membrane

  • Astrocyte end-feet

Astrocyte functions:

  • Maintain BBB

  • Provide metabolic support to neurons

  • Maintain extracellular ion balance

  • Repair and scar formation (gliosis)

Anatomy-02.question: ২০) The most abundant type of cerebral cortical neurons is the
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is pyramidal cell. Pyramidal neurons are the most abundant projection neurons of the cerebral cortex and are the principal output cells of the cortex. Their axons form important pathways such as the corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine tracts.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Purkinje cell – A characteristic neuron of the cerebellar cortex, not the cerebral cortex. It provides inhibitory output from the cerebellar cortex.

  • Stellate cell – Present in the cerebral cortex, especially in the granular layers, but they are less numerous than pyramidal cells.

  • Fusiform cell – Found mainly in the deeper layers of the cerebral cortex and contributes to cortical output, but is not the most abundant type.

High-yield points:

Major neurons of cerebral cortex:

  • Pyramidal cells → most abundant, projection neurons

  • Stellate cells → interneurons

  • Fusiform cells → deep cortical layers

Cerebellar cortex characteristic neuron:

  • Purkinje cell

Anatomy-02.question: ২১) Predominant cell type of epidermis
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is keratinocyte. Keratinocytes are the predominant cells of the epidermis, making up about 90–95% of epidermal cells. They produce keratin, a structural protein that provides strength, protection, and waterproofing to the skin.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Melanocyte – Produces melanin pigment responsible for skin colour and protection against ultraviolet radiation. They are present mainly in the basal layer but are much fewer in number.

  • Langerhans cell – An antigen-presenting immune cell of the epidermis involved in immune surveillance.

  • Merkel cell – A mechanoreceptor cell involved in light touch sensation, associated with sensory nerve endings.

High-yield points:

Cells of epidermis:

  • Keratinocyte → Most abundant; produces keratin

  • Melanocyte → Produces melanin

  • Langerhans cell → Immune function

  • Merkel cell → Touch sensation

Epidermal layers (deep to superficial):
Basale → Spinosum → Granulosum → (Lucidum in thick skin) → Corneum

Anatomy-02.question: ২২) Which type of papillae contains most taste bud
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is circumvallate papillae. Although circumvallate papillae are few in number (about 8–12), each papilla contains a large number of taste buds, making them the papillae with the greatest concentration of taste buds.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Filiform – Most numerous papillae of the tongue but do not contain taste buds. They mainly provide mechanical function.

  • Fungiform – Contain taste buds, especially near the tip and margins of the tongue, but fewer compared with circumvallate papillae.

  • Foliate – Contain taste buds and are located on the posterolateral margins of the tongue, but are less prominent in humans.

High-yield points:

  • Most numerous papillae → Filiform

  • Largest papillae → Circumvallate

  • Most taste buds → Circumvallate

  • No taste buds → Filiform

  • Taste bud-containing papillae → Fungiform, Foliate, Circumvallate

Anatomy-02.question: ২৩) Blood supply of middle cerebral artery-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is temporal pole. The middle cerebral artery (MCA) supplies the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including the temporal pole.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Medial surface of cerebral cortex – Supplied mainly by the anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

  • Motor area including leg area – The leg area of the motor cortex lies on the medial surface (paracentral lobule) and is supplied by the ACA. MCA supplies the lateral motor cortex (face and upper limb areas).

  • Visual cortex – Supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA).

High-yield points:

Cerebral artery territories:

Middle cerebral artery (MCA):

  • Lateral surface of cerebral hemisphere

  • Motor cortex: face and upper limb areas

  • Sensory cortex: face and upper limb areas

  • Broca and Wernicke areas (dominant hemisphere)

  • Temporal pole

Anterior cerebral artery (ACA):

  • Medial frontal and parietal lobes

  • Leg area of motor and sensory cortex

Posterior cerebral artery (PCA):

  • Occipital lobe

  • Visual cortex

  • Inferomedial temporal lobe**

Anatomy-02.question: ২৪) Function of limbic system excludes-
Anatomy-02.option3: Influence reaction to fear and anger
Anatomy-02.option4: Convert recent memory to long term memory
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is influence reproductive system. The limbic system mainly regulates emotions, behaviour, motivation, and memory. It can influence sexual behaviour and emotional responses, but direct control of the reproductive system is primarily a function of the hypothalamus and endocrine system.

The other options are associated with limbic system functions:

  • Influence sexual behavior – True. The limbic system, especially the hypothalamus and amygdala, plays a role in sexual behaviour and motivation.

  • Influence reaction to fear and anger – True. The amygdala is important in emotional responses, especially fear and aggression.

  • Convert recent memory to long-term memory – True. The hippocampus is responsible for consolidation of recent memory into long-term memory.

High-yield points:

Functions of limbic system:

  • Emotion (fear, anger, pleasure)

  • Behaviour and motivation

  • Sexual behaviour

  • Memory formation and consolidation

  • Reward mechanisms

Key structures:

  • Hippocampus → memory consolidation

  • Amygdala → fear and emotional responses

  • Hypothalamus → autonomic and endocrine responses

Anatomy-02.question: ২৫) Which supplies nourishment to retina
২৬) Nucleus of hypothalamus involved in controlling circadian rhythms
২৭) Lateral surface of cerebrum is mainly supplied by
২৮) Neuroglial cell located in peripheral nerves
২৯) Multipolar neuron
৩০) The structures providing structural support to astrocytes -
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is intermediate filament. Astrocytes contain glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an intermediate filament that provides structural support and mechanical strength to astrocytes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Microfilament – Mainly involved in cell movement, contraction, and cytoskeletal changes; not the main structural support in astrocytes.

  • Microtubule – Important for intracellular transport and maintenance of cell shape, but not the characteristic structural filament of astrocytes.

  • Secondary filament – Not a recognized cytoskeletal component in astrocytes.

High-yield points:

Astrocyte marker:

  • GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) → intermediate filament

Functions of astrocytes:

  • Maintain blood–brain barrier

  • Provide structural support to neurons

  • Regulate extracellular potassium

  • Repair CNS injury by gliosis

  • Provide metabolic support to neurons

Key association:

  • Astrocyte → GFAP → Intermediate filament

  • Oligodendrocyte → CNS myelin

  • Schwann cell → PNS myelin

  • Microglia → CNS macrophage

  • Ependymal cell → CSF lining cells

Anatomy-02.question: ৩১) What term applies to collections of neuronal cell bodies (somata) outside the central nervous system?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is ganglia. A ganglion (plural: ganglia) is a collection of neuronal cell bodies (somata) located outside the central nervous system (CNS), i.e., in the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neuroglia – Supportive cells of the nervous system, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells, and Schwann cells.

  • Nodes – Refers mainly to nodes of Ranvier, gaps between segments of myelin sheath along axons where saltatory conduction occurs.

  • Nuclei – Collections of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS (e.g., basal ganglia nuclei, thalamic nuclei).

High-yield points:

  • Ganglia → Collection of neuron cell bodies in PNS

  • Nuclei → Collection of neuron cell bodies in CNS

  • Tract → Bundle of axons in CNS

  • Nerve → Bundle of axons in PNS

Anatomy-02.question: ৩২) Branches of internal carotid artery-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is posterior communicating artery. The internal carotid artery (ICA) gives several important intracranial branches, including:

  • Ophthalmic artery

  • Posterior communicating artery

  • Anterior choroidal artery

  • Superior hypophyseal arteries

  • Terminal branches: anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Anterior communicating artery – Connects the two anterior cerebral arteries and is part of the circle of Willis, but it is not a direct branch of the internal carotid artery.

  • Meningeal branch – Meningeal branches are mainly derived from the external carotid artery (e.g., middle meningeal artery), not a typical branch of the ICA.

  • Pontine artery – Arises mainly from the basilar artery, supplying the pons.

High-yield points:

Branches of internal carotid artery:

  • Ophthalmic artery

  • Posterior communicating artery

  • Anterior choroidal artery

  • Superior hypophyseal arteries

  • ACA

  • MCA

Circle of Willis:

  • ACA + anterior communicating artery

  • Internal carotid arteries

  • Posterior communicating arteries

  • Posterior cerebral arteries

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৩) Incorrect about Hypothalamus-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is controls voluntary movement. The hypothalamus does not control voluntary movements; this function is mainly performed by the motor cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum.

The other options are true functions of the hypothalamus:

  • Regulate body temperature – The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat. The anterior hypothalamus promotes heat loss, while the posterior hypothalamus promotes heat conservation.

  • Controls emotion and behavior – The hypothalamus interacts with the limbic system and regulates emotional responses, motivation, and behavioural patterns.

  • Has endocrine function – The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland through releasing and inhibiting hormones and produces ADH and oxytocin.

High-yield points:

Functions of hypothalamus:

  • Temperature regulation

  • Water balance and thirst

  • Hunger and satiety

  • Endocrine control (pituitary regulation)

  • Autonomic nervous system regulation

  • Sleep–wake cycle (suprachiasmatic nucleus)

  • Emotional and behavioural responses

Voluntary movement → Motor cortex + basal ganglia + cerebellum

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৪) A boy falls from height on out stretched hand after some days his thenar muscles is found wasting, which nerve is most commonly affected?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is median nerve. A fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) can cause a supracondylar fracture of the humerus or wrist injury, which may damage the median nerve. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles through its recurrent branch; injury leads to thenar muscle wasting and impaired thumb opposition.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Brachial plexus – Can be injured in shoulder trauma, but isolated thenar wasting most commonly indicates median nerve involvement.

  • Radial nerve – Supplies wrist and finger extensors; injury causes wrist drop, not thenar wasting.

  • Ulnar nerve – Supplies hypothenar muscles and most intrinsic hand muscles; injury causes claw hand and interosseous wasting.

High-yield points:

Median nerve injury:

  • Thenar wasting

  • Loss of thumb opposition

  • Ape thumb deformity

  • Sensory loss over lateral 3½ fingers

Ulnar nerve injury:

  • Interosseous wasting

  • Claw hand

  • Loss of finger abduction/adduction

Radial nerve injury:

  • Wrist drop

  • Loss of extension movements

FOOSH injury → think supracondylar fracture → median nerve (common association)

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৫) Which is a part of epithalamus-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is habenular nucleus. The epithalamus is a part of the dorsal diencephalon and includes:

  • Pineal gland

  • Habenular nuclei

  • Stria medullaris thalami

  • Posterior commissure

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Caudate nucleus – A component of the basal ganglia, involved in motor control and learning.

  • Anterior commissure – A commissural fibre tract connecting parts of the two cerebral hemispheres, mainly related to olfactory and temporal lobe connections; not a part of the epithalamus.

  • Septum pellucidum – A thin membrane separating the lateral ventricles, associated with the septal area of the limbic system.

High-yield points:

Diencephalon divisions:

  • Thalamus → sensory relay

  • Hypothalamus → autonomic, endocrine, homeostasis

  • Epithalamus → pineal gland + habenular nuclei

  • Subthalamus → motor pathway connections

Habenular nucleus functions:

  • Limbic system connection

  • Regulation of emotional and behavioural responses

  • Reward and aversion pathways

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৬) A patient having a tumor on the medial wall of the body of the lateral ventricle will involve which of the following structure?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is septum pellucidum. The medial wall of the body of the lateral ventricle is formed mainly by the septum pellucidum. Therefore, a tumour arising from this location is most likely to involve the septum pellucidum.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Caudate nucleus – Forms the lateral wall of the body of the lateral ventricle, not the medial wall.

  • Corpus callosum – Forms the roof of the body of the lateral ventricle.

  • Thalamus – Forms part of the floor of the central part of the lateral ventricle (mainly the posterior part).

High-yield points:

Walls of the body of lateral ventricle:

  • Roof → Corpus callosum

  • Medial wall → Septum pellucidum

  • Lateral wall → Caudate nucleus

  • Floor → Thalamus + choroid plexus + fornix

Clinical correlation:

  • Tumour near lateral ventricle → symptoms due to obstruction of CSF flow → hydrocephalus.

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৭) Brodmann’s number given to auditosensory area is-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is Brodmann areas 41 and 42. The auditory (audiosensory) cortex is located in the superior temporal gyrus and corresponds to primary auditory cortex (BA 41) and auditory association cortex (BA 42).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 44,45 – Represent Broca’s area, the motor speech area in the dominant frontal lobe.

  • 3,1,2 – Represent the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.

  • 18,19 – Represent the visual association cortex in the occipital lobe.

High-yield points:

Important Brodmann areas:

  • BA 4 → Primary motor cortex

  • BA 3,1,2 → Primary somatosensory cortex

  • BA 17 → Primary visual cortex

  • BA 18,19 → Visual association cortex

  • BA 41,42 → Auditory cortex

  • BA 44,45 → Broca’s motor speech area

  • BA 22 → Wernicke’s sensory speech area

Auditory cortex location: Superior temporal gyrus (transverse temporal gyri of Heschl)

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৮) Corpus callosum is the largest commissural fibre that connects the hemispheres. which of the following area is not connected by corpus callosum?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is hippocampus. The corpus callosum connects corresponding neocortical areas of the two cerebral hemispheres. The hippocampus is an allocortical (limbic) structure and is not connected primarily by the corpus callosum. It communicates mainly through the fornix and hippocampal commissure.

The other options are connected by corpus callosum:

  • Auditory area – The auditory cortices of both hemispheres have interconnections through commissural fibres.

  • Broca’s area – The dominant and non-dominant frontal language areas are connected through corpus callosum.

  • Visual cortex – Visual association areas are connected mainly through the splenium of corpus callosum.

High-yield points:

Corpus callosum connects:

  • Frontal lobes → genu

  • Parietal and temporal lobes → body

  • Occipital lobes (visual areas) → splenium

Not typically connected by corpus callosum:

  • Hippocampus (limbic system) → mainly connected via fornix

Note: The corpus callosum mainly connects neocortex, not deeper limbic structures.

Anatomy-02.question: ৩৯) A lesion of the posterior limb of the internal capsule on the right may result in-
Anatomy-02.option2: A drooping of the corner of the mouth on the right
Anatomy-02.option3: UMN type of paralysis of the left side of body
Anatomy-02.option4: A left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is UMN type of paralysis of the left side of body. The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains the corticospinal tract, which carries motor fibres from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord. Since these fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla, a lesion of the right posterior limb causes contralateral (left-sided) upper motor neuron weakness.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Transcortical apraxia – Usually results from lesions of the supplementary motor area or parietal association cortex, not the internal capsule.

  • Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the right – A right internal capsule lesion affects left corticobulbar fibres, causing left lower facial weakness, not right-sided drooping.

  • Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing – Occurs due to lesions of the right occipital visual cortex supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. The optic radiation in the internal capsule (retrolentiform part) may cause visual field defects, but macular sparing is a cortical feature.

High-yield points:

Internal capsule contents:

  • Anterior limb

    • Frontopontine fibres

    • Anterior thalamic radiation

  • Genu

    • Corticobulbar fibres

  • Posterior limb

    • Corticospinal fibres → contralateral hemiplegia

    • Sensory thalamocortical fibres

  • Retrolentiform part

    • Optic radiation → homonymous hemianopia

  • Sublentiform part

    • Auditory radiation

Classic internal capsule lesion:
→ Contralateral face, arm, and leg weakness (pure motor stroke)

Anatomy-02.question: ৪০) Each of the following vessels empties into the coronary sinus except the :
Anatomy-02.option4: posterior vein of the left ventricle
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is anterior cardiac vein. The anterior cardiac veins do not drain into the coronary sinus; instead, they drain directly into the right atrium.

The other options drain into the coronary sinus:

  • Great cardiac vein – Drains into the left end of the coronary sinus; accompanies the anterior interventricular artery.

  • Middle cardiac vein – Drains into the coronary sinus; accompanies the posterior interventricular artery.

  • Posterior vein of the left ventricle – Drains into the coronary sinus.

High-yield points:

Tributaries of coronary sinus:

  • Great cardiac vein

  • Middle cardiac vein

  • Small cardiac vein

  • Posterior vein(s) of left ventricle

  • Oblique vein of left atrium

Veins draining directly into right atrium:

  • Anterior cardiac veins

  • Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins)

Coronary sinus → Opens into right atrium

Anatomy-02.question: ৪১) The left coronary artery bifurcates into the circumflex branch & the :
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is anterior interventricular branch (left anterior descending artery, LAD). The left coronary artery (LCA) usually divides into two major branches:

  • Anterior interventricular artery (LAD)

  • Circumflex artery (LCx)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Left marginal branch – Usually arises from the circumflex artery and supplies the left ventricular lateral wall.

  • Right marginal branch – A branch of the right coronary artery, supplying the right ventricular margin.

  • Posterior interventricular branch – Usually arises from the right coronary artery (in right-dominant circulation) and runs in the posterior interventricular sulcus.

High-yield points:

Left coronary artery branches:

  • Anterior interventricular artery (LAD)

  • Circumflex artery

LAD supplies:

  • Anterior interventricular septum

  • Anterior wall of left ventricle

  • Bundle branches of conduction system

Circumflex artery supplies:

  • Lateral wall of left ventricle

  • Left atrium

Classic exam association:

  • LAD = "widow maker" artery (proximal LAD occlusion can cause extensive anterior MI)

Anatomy-02.question: ৪২) Each of the following is related to the right ventricle except the :
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is bicuspid valve (mitral valve). The bicuspid/mitral valve is related to the left ventricle, not the right ventricle. It lies between the left atrium and left ventricle.

The other options are related to the right ventricle:

  • Interventricular septum – Forms part of the medial wall of the right ventricle and separates it from the left ventricle.

  • Trabeculae carneae – Irregular muscular ridges present in the ventricular walls, including the right ventricle.

  • Anterior papillary muscle – A papillary muscle of the right ventricle that attaches to the cusps of the tricuspid valve via chordae tendineae.

High-yield points:

Right ventricle:

  • Tricuspid valve

  • Trabeculae carneae

  • Three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, septal)

  • Moderator band

  • Pulmonary valve

Left ventricle:

  • Bicuspid (mitral) valve

  • Two papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial)

  • Thickest myocardium

Anatomy-02.question: ৪৩) Which forms an electrical “barrier” between the atria and ventricles so that they contract independently?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is fibrous skeleton. The cardiac fibrous skeleton forms an electrical insulation barrier between the atria and ventricles, preventing direct conduction of impulses from atrial myocardium to ventricular myocardium. The electrical impulse can normally pass only through the atrioventricular (AV) node and bundle of His.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • SAN (sinoatrial node) – The primary pacemaker of the heart; initiates atrial contraction but does not act as an electrical barrier.

  • AVN (atrioventricular node) – Delays conduction between atria and ventricles, allowing ventricular filling, but it is not the insulating barrier.

  • Papillary muscle – Prevents valve prolapse during ventricular contraction through chordae tendineae; it has no role in electrical isolation.

High-yield points:

Cardiac fibrous skeleton functions:

  • Provides structural support for valves

  • Acts as electrical insulation between atria and ventricles

  • Allows conduction mainly through AV node → Bundle of His

Normal conduction pathway:
SA node → Atrial myocardium → AV node → Bundle of His → Right & left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

Anatomy-02.question: ৪৪) Which cardiac vein drains directly into Right atrium?
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is anterior cardiac vein. The anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium rather than joining the coronary sinus.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Great cardiac vein – Drains into the coronary sinus.

  • Middle cardiac vein – Drains into the coronary sinus.

  • Small cardiac vein – Drains into the coronary sinus.

High-yield points:

Cardiac venous drainage:

Into coronary sinus:

  • Great cardiac vein

  • Middle cardiac vein

  • Small cardiac vein

  • Posterior vein of left ventricle

  • Oblique vein of left atrium

Directly into right atrium:

  • Anterior cardiac veins

  • Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins)

Coronary sinus → Opens into right atrium

Anatomy-02.question: ৪৫) Location of windowed capillaries
৪৬) Membranous labyrinth consists of –
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is utricle. The membranous labyrinth is a system of fluid-filled membranous structures within the bony labyrinth of the inner ear. It includes:

  • Utricle

  • Saccule

  • Semicircular ducts

  • Cochlear duct

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Semicircular canal – The bony labyrinth contains semicircular canals, while the membranous counterpart is semicircular ducts.

  • Vestibule – A part of the bony labyrinth containing the utricle and saccule.

  • Oval window – An opening in the middle ear that transmits vibrations from the stapes to the inner ear; not part of the labyrinth.

High-yield points:

Bony labyrinth:

  • Cochlea

  • Vestibule

  • Semicircular canals

Membranous labyrinth:

  • Cochlear duct

  • Utricle

  • Saccule

  • Semicircular ducts

Mnemonic:
Membranous = Ducts + Utricle + Saccule (DUS)

Anatomy-02.question: ৪৭) Tributaries of the cavernous sinus exclude -
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is superior petrosal sinus. The superior petrosal sinus is not a tributary of the cavernous sinus; rather, it is a continuation/drainage pathway from the cavernous sinus, carrying blood from the cavernous sinus to the transverse sinus.

The other options are tributaries of the cavernous sinus:

  • Sphenoparietal sinus – Drains into the cavernous sinus.

  • Superficial middle cerebral vein – Drains into the cavernous sinus through connections on the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere.

  • Superior ophthalmic vein – A major tributary of the cavernous sinus, draining blood from the orbit.

High-yield points:

Tributaries of cavernous sinus:

  • Superior ophthalmic vein

  • Inferior ophthalmic vein

  • Superficial middle cerebral vein

  • Sphenoparietal sinus

  • Central vein of retina

Connections/drainage from cavernous sinus:

  • Superior petrosal sinus → transverse sinus

  • Inferior petrosal sinus → internal jugular vein

Clinical correlation:
Cavernous sinus thrombosis may cause:

  • Ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI involvement)

  • Loss of facial sensation (V1, V2)

  • Proptosis and orbital congestion

Anatomy-02.question: ৪৮) Tactile epithelial cell of skin-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is Merkel cells. Merkel cells (tactile epithelial cells) are specialized sensory cells present in the basal layer of the epidermis. They function as mechanoreceptors involved in fine touch sensation and are associated with sensory nerve endings.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Keratinocytes – Most abundant cells of the epidermis; produce keratin and form the protective barrier of skin.

  • Melanocytes – Produce melanin pigment responsible for skin colour and protection against UV radiation.

  • Langerhans cells – Antigen-presenting immune cells involved in immune surveillance of the skin.

High-yield points:

Cells of epidermis:

  • Keratinocyte → Keratin production, most abundant

  • Melanocyte → Melanin production

  • Langerhans cell → Immune function

  • Merkel cell → Touch sensation (tactile cell)

Merkel cell location: Stratum basale of epidermis.

Anatomy-02.question: ৪৯) The capillaries are-
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is exchange vessels. Capillaries are the primary sites of exchange between blood and tissues, allowing movement of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, and metabolic waste products.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Distribution vessels – Mainly refers to arteries, which distribute blood from the heart to different organs.

  • Resistance vessels – Mainly refers to arterioles, which regulate blood flow and blood pressure by changing vascular resistance.

  • Capacitance or reservoir vessels – Refers to veins, which store a large volume of blood and return it to the heart.

High-yield points:

Classification of blood vessels:

Vessel Main function
Arteries Distribution vessels
Arterioles Resistance vessels
Capillaries Exchange vessels
Veins Capacitance/reservoir vessels

Capillaries:

  • Single layer of endothelial cells

  • Site of exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products

Anatomy-02.question: ৫০) Pachymeninx is -
Anatomy-02.exp:
The correct answer is dura mater. The pachymeninx (pachymeninges) refers to the thick, tough outer meningeal layer, which is the dura mater.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Arachnoid mater – A thin, delicate middle meningeal layer; together with pia mater forms the leptomeninges.

  • Pia mater – A thin inner meningeal layer that closely adheres to the surface of the brain and spinal cord.

  • Part of basal ganglia – Not related to the meninges.

High-yield points:

Meningeal layers:

  • Pachymeninx → Dura mater (thick membrane)

  • Leptomeninges → Arachnoid mater + Pia mater (thin membranes)

Dural specializations:

  • Forms dural folds (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli)

  • Contains dural venous sinuses

Clinical correlation:

  • Epidural hematoma → between skull and dura

  • Subdural hematoma → between dura and arachnoid

  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage → between arachnoid and pia
